body_markdown:
Between the 13th and 14th salary, e-EFKA contributions, and tenure-based notice periods, Greek labor law asks for more than most founders expect when they plan a first hire. You don’t have to learn all of it yourself. An employer of record in Greece takes on those obligations directly, so we’re breaking down what that looks like and how it compares to setting up your own entity.


**TLDR:**


- An EOR hires Greek workers on your behalf, skipping entity setup entirely.
- Greek employers owe 13th/14th salary bonuses plus ~21.79% (OECD, 2026) e-EFKA contributions.
- Notice periods run 1 month at 1-4 years' tenure up to 4 months at 10+ years.
- Entity setup costs stay fixed regardless of hire count; EOR fees scale per person.
- Bolto positions itself as an EOR for Greece, handling contracts, payroll, and e-EFKA filings.


## What Is an Employer of Record in Greece


An[Employer of Record (EOR)](https://www.bolto.com/blog/eor-definition-employer-of-record) in Greece is a locally licensed legal employer that hires Greek workers on your behalf, so you can build a team there without registering a Greek branch or subsidiary. The EOR appears on the employment contract and payroll records as the legal employer, handles filings with[e-EFKA, the national social security fund](https://www.gov.gr/en/organizations/ministries/upourgeio-ergasias-kai-koinonikes-asphalises/elektronikos-ethnikos-phoreas-koinonikes-asphalises-e-ephka) , and registers the employment relationship with Ergani, the national labor registry. You keep control of the actual work: setting goals, directing projects, and managing performance day to day.


Greek entity registration generally takes weeks and involves tax authority filings, local bank setup, and ongoing corporate compliance that outlasts a single hire. An EOR sidesteps that timeline entirely.


Companies generally turn to this structure when:


- Testing the Greek market before committing to a permanent legal presence
- Hiring one specialist or a small team, where entity setup costs would outweigh the benefit
- Needing someone onboarded quickly, without waiting on registration paperwork


In each case, the[employer of record services](https://www.bolto.com/blog/employer-of-record-services-how-to-choose) carry the legal and administrative weight of Greek employment law, while you stay focused on running the work itself.


## Employment Laws and Compliance Requirements in Greece


Under Greek labor law, employers generally take on obligations that go beyond base salary. Employees typically receive a 13th salary as a Christmas bonus, plus a 14th salary split between an Easter allowance and a summer holiday allowance. Employers also contribute around 21.79% (OECD, 2026) of gross salary to e-EFKA, Greece’s unified social security fund, up to the monthly contribution cap, with employees contributing separately from their own pay.


[Notice periods in Greece](https://ypergasias.gov.gr/en/labour-relations/individual-employment-relations/frequently-asked-questions/) generally scale with tenure, starting at 1 month for one to four years of service and rising to 4 months at ten or more years. Severance typically applies after 12 months of continuous employment, and doubles if the notice period is skipped. Probation periods allow more flexible termination terms during the initial months of employment, though specifics can vary by contract and industry.


These rules shift over time and can depend on contract type, sector, and individual circumstances. Working through an EOR means the EOR handles these calculations, filings, and deadlines on the employer’s behalf.

## Cost of Hiring in Greece with an EOR vs. a Local Entity


Setting up a Greek entity means registering with the General Commercial Registry (GEMI), enrolling with the tax authority AADE, and registering as an employer with e-EFKA before anyone can go on payroll. Add local accounting support, legal counsel for compliant contracts, and compliance staff time, and the overhead builds before you hire anyone.


That overhead does not shrink for a small hire. Whether you bring on one person or five, entity formation costs, registry fees, and retainers stay largely the same. An EOR changes that math: costs scale per employee, so hiring one person in Greece costs roughly what one hire costs, without the weight of a branch you barely use.

## EOR vs. Local Entity in Greece: Which Is Right for You


Choosing between an EOR and a local entity in Greece generally comes down to timing and commitment, beyond cost alone. An EOR gets a Greek hire onboarded fast, with the EOR handling e-EFKA contributions, the 13th and 14th salary payments, and notice periods, though you give up some control over benefits customization and equity design along the way. A local entity gives you full control over compensation structure and equity, and it can cost less per employee once you’ve scaled past a handful of hires, but it also means absorbing GEMI registration, AADE tax setup, and the ongoing compliance overhead that comes with running a Greek subsidiary. Here’s how that tradeoff plays out in practice.


The right choice generally comes down to how committed you are to the Greek market and how many people you plan to hire there.


If you’re testing demand with one or two roles, need someone onboarded quickly, or aren’t ready to commit to a long-term legal presence, an EOR lets you skip GEMI registration, AADE tax setup, and e-EFKA employer enrollment while still paying your team on time and in compliance with Greek labor rules.


If you’re planning to scale a larger team in Greece, want full control over equity and benefits design, or expect Greece to become a permanent base for the business, a local entity can make more sense once you’ve absorbed the setup timeline and ongoing compliance overhead that comes with it.


Many companies start with an EOR to get a first hire started fast, then revisit the entity decision later as headcount and long-term commitment grow. The two approaches aren’t mutually exclusive: an EOR can serve as the on-ramp that buys time to make the entity decision without pressure to get it right on day one.
